INTERVIEW
OF
ARTHUR BRIGGS
By James Lincoln Collier

S. & S. REPORTING CO., INC.
Court Reporters—Notaries
132 Nassau Street
New York City
WOrth 2-2915
2943
Briggs 2
Okay, if you have no objection, let's go right back to the beginning; when were you born and where were you born and what was your family?
I was born in Charleston, South Carolina the 10th of April, 1901. My parents were from Grenada, Mississippi.
Grenada?
Grenada, Mississippi.
Is that somewhere in the Delta country, was it? Was that the Delta country?
Yes, it certainly was.* I was brought up in Charleston.
What did your Dad do down there?
He was a sanitary inspector.
In Charleston?
In Charleston. And what you call a preacher as well, just as Ol' Man Jenkins was.
*Grenada, Mississippi is in central Mississippi.
Briggs
Right.
They were both not ordained, but they were preachers.
And what else do you want to know?
Well, your mother, did she work as well or was she --
No, my mother didn't work.
Right, she --
I'm the last of eleven children.
Eleven children.
I can see there's good reason why she didn't work.
And there was a difference of three years between children, say --
Well, when were your parents born. They must have been born way back.
Well, I think my Dad was born somewhere around '58 or something.
He was.
Yes, 1858, or something.
Briggs
And your mother must have been born near enough for --
Yeh, pretty close, yes.
Okay, so, now, -- but Charleston was a fairly big town by that time or not too big?
Yes, Charleston was a, pretty -- yes, pretty well known, more or less,-- quite a lot of poverty and naturally--- but it was prospering, how do you say, prospering, yes.

And, I don't know, it seems that, as though quite a few things were happening in Charleston. I was more or less too young to realize what was going on, and as far as that's concerned, children never worry about what's happening, you know, they just --
Right.
-- live, try to live and do the best they can.
That was a period when things were getting tougher for blacks
Briggs
Yes, it was pretty rough, but there were patrons who were pretty nice to the blacks.
There were --
Yes, there were. Quite a few.
In what way, I mean, they'd --

In helping them to -- in the education and everything else, (Inaudible) Education and everything else they tried to -- and that's really what helped Mr. Jenkins and the way he was sponsored and helped, you see, to organize his --
Right. In other words he was getting -- most of his support was being raised by whites?
By whites, oh, yes, yes.
They kept the thing going by donations, but also he was making
Briggs
some money with the band.

Right, he did make a whole lot of money. I mean that's a question I don't want to discuss. That question -- because I'm not sure. It's said that he made quite a lot of money. He was a millionaire when he died.
Really, was that known or --
Yes, more or less, yes.
Because it was, -- I know that's been said. He was taking and putting some of that in his pocket.

Yes, he -- but I think it was, as far as I'm concerned, his son didn't say much when we tried to find out certain things from him, but he didn't say much -- but he was not on very good terms with his father.
I see.
Briggs
Social reasons, for social reasons. Probably that had something to do with it. He did not appreciate the treatment of orphans in the band.
The son?
The son. He didn't -- he didn't appreciate -- but I learned through the two boys who worked with me that Patrick Brothers, the cousin....
Who were in the band?
Who were in the band. And Edmund Jenkins himself, was very, very familiar with those two boys.
Right.

He happened to know them because they were youngsters when he left, and I believe Patrick was -- yes, Patrick was a member of the band that came over with Jenkins when Edmund stayed to continue his musical studies.
Briggs
I see.
That was in fourteen.
Let me just take you back, so I can get the dates here straight. So, were you associated with that band at all or just knew about it?
No. I knew about it for the simple reason that Mr. ---the man who taught me music, Mr. Eugene Mikell was a teacher, one of the teachers of the Jenkins Orphanage.
I see.
But he had also private pupils, and I was one of -- well, I became one of his private pupils, you see.
I see.

So I knew of the orphanage and I knew just what he was doing, because he even stretched his musical intuition to the churches, organized bands and things, to take the youngsters in hand and teach them
Briggs
Right.
But private, you see.
Right.
'Cause through the churches, our parents had enough money to pay --
Well, your Dad had a pretty good job down there, for a black --
Yes, very good. He was a sanitary inspector. He was not what you would call a principal sanitary. He was under, you know, control.
Right.
He had a position in the Sanitary Department.
But he wasn't working day labor like most of the blacks down there?
No, no, no, not scavenger work.
Right.
No, he had a more or
Briggs
Right.
I couldn't say what type of job he had, but I think he was a -- he had a pretty good education.
He did?
Yes, I think the people who were taking care of his parents, grandparents, you know, they were pretty good to him and his family.
I see. Well, I have just again to go back a little bit, he was actually -- he and your Mom were actually born as slaves?
Oh yes. Yes, surely (Laughter).
So they could have remembered even another time?
Yes. As far as they were concerned, Dad never spoke to us about what happened.
He didn't?
Briggs
No. And that is, I think, something I inherited from Dad, 'cause I never think of talk a lot.
I believe that men are men and I judge men by their actions, you see. That's the way I have always felt. That's the way I have always acted in my professional activities.

You see, I've had -- under certain circumstances, some of the boys have asked me, 'Why don't you take so and so, and so and so.' And I said, 'No, I take so and so and so and so, because I want so and so.'
You see. And that happens -- I have been not ostracized, but almost, on account of that, you see.
You see, you realize that the majority of the musicians I've had with me were just men. That's the way I consider it.
They acted towards me too, as men and I acted towards them -- I had that, as though it were a little fluid or something that
Briggs
drew me to them, in both ways, and vice-versa you see, --
Because there was a personal feeling.
Yes, a personal feeling. And I'll just give you a little example.
The piano I have, at home.
This is a very nice grand piano that is in the living room.
Yes, that piano was sold to me -- I say "sold," it was almost given to me, by a pianist who worked with me way back in 1923, a Frenchman.
He became the manager and director of one of the biggest butter firms in France after. His name was Louis Bergerér.
Right.
He died while three years ago I was with him, not every day until his death, but I was with him most always.
Because we caught up with each other--
Briggs
I'm a little nervous, I don't know why. 'Cause I haven't spoken like this --
Don't worry about it. We're just talking.
We caught up with each other, we found each other, it was an accident, through a friend. He, being manager-director of this big butter company -- what's the name of it -- Privado.
Right.

Privado Butter Company in France, and during the conversation he had with someone, they mentioned that they had seen at the Chez Florence Cabaret in Paris after liberation, because he, Bergerér, I think he managed to get -- he went to the States, he managed to get to New York before the Germans came in. And he said --'Chez Florence, I had a very good friend, I know he was at Chez Florence from 1946 on. His name was Arthur
Briggs 14

Briggs and he had an orchestra --." The person said, "Why sure, Arthur, I know him well, I've been a patron in the place, I can contact him and find out.--," you know. Then Louis told him about how we met way back and worked together and everything else. Then we made a contact and he asked me out to his home, and he lived in very, very fine suburbs of Paris, at Pol Le Deux (??). That's near Versailles. Beaugerval, Beau Crescent, near Versailles. And he invited us to his home and I took my wife and my daughter with me, and he had this piano in the livingroom. He said to me, "Art," he said, "Do you remember." I said, "Sure." He said, "I'm going to play you something. I'm going to play you something you'd probably like to hear one of Chopin's, La Baroque Polonaise." So, I told him, I said, "Look, Louis,
Briggs

my daughter has just started piano, but we have no instrument." I said, "For the time being, I hope I'll be able to get a piano, because she would not progress unless she has an instrument so she can practice at home."
So, he said, "Art," he said, "You have a piano." I said, "What do you mean?" He said, "Well, it's yours." And I said, "Now look, that's out." He said, "Yes, for your daughter."

He called my daughter over. "Barbara, come over." And she sat at the piano and she started playing tunes that she learned with her teacher, you see, and he said, "Art, when are you going to come and get it, the piano."

I said, "No, that's out." I said, "If you want to sell it to me, if you want to make it a price, I'll accept it," but I said, "But Louis, I couldn't --". "Wonderful piano, reconstructed and everything else."
Briggs 16
And he said, 'Well, look, this has been around here, about eight years ago.' And I forced him to take 200,000 francs, which is nothing in comparison --
Right.
Wonderful piano.
Sure.
And I made out a check to his wife whom I'd known at the same time. We were all more or less youngsters together, you see.

And she said, 'Art, I'm going to have a lot of trouble with Lou. Lulu, as we called him, 'Because he won't be satisfied, otherwise.' I said, 'You're going to have to keep your piano, I don't want it.'
So, I said, 'He offered to pay the transportation and everything else.' I said, 'Now, look, that's out.'
Well, it so happened that she managed to, his wife -- I'm in contact with her
Briggs 17
right through. Send Christmas cards and call her sometimes. She lives in Le Havre now.
Right.

And I -- we arranged, I sent transportation to have it brought--brought the piano here and gave her a check. And Louis was doing pretty good, but he -- I don't think he -- he was just a person who thought he was sick, imaginary sick.
I see.

You see. But it finally got the best of him. 'Cause he told me, he said, "Art, I have that dreaded disease." So I said, "You're crazy." I said, "Just take a look at yourself in the mirror, and you'll see that --". So, he said, "I don't know," he said, "You're with me all the while," he said, "but at nights I have awful pains." I said, "You can, you're not a spring chicken, you know." (Laughter).
Briggs

So, I don't know what was the matter really, 'cause it was his illness, but he kept on ailing, and taking his retirement. That played a pretty hard -- I mean, his retirement worried him to death. He did not take his retirement. The youngsters came in and they forced him, you see.
Sure.

And he was awfully hurt, because he called me and told me, he said, "Art," he said, -- it's awkward --, he said, "The way they used -- just roughed me out, it's just one of those things, they tell me get out, you know."
Right.
"As though I was nothing." Well, all that worked on him and he finally died about three years ago.
So that was how, the relationship with the --
The piano. Yes, that's why I have it. He was a French boy.
Briggs
And my relationships in general, just as I've told you, most of the orchestras I've had, have been, I select the men myself.
Right.
And I did not accept a job if the proprietor tried to tell me to take so and so, and so and so.
Right.

It happened just once to me, way back in London, when I went to Oslo. The proprietor of the Hotel Bristol, Mr. Jensen, imposed a pianist on me. That was okay, it didn't make any difference. But this person, it so happened he was a, he was not a genial person.
Right.
We went to Oslo and I don't generally criticize musicians 'cause I feel if you're good, you're okay, and if you're not good, you have to live. You see, that's the way I've always been. You
Briggs
maybe don't make the grade but you have to live as a human being, and if you try your best, you're okay.
Well, this guy, as far as I'm concerned, he was really the world's worst pianist.
Really.
(Laughter). He couldn't read, he couldn't play. He was never an instrumentalist. He never studied, and he knew nothing about the instrument.

But the worst thing about him is this -- I don't like to say things like this, but I have to tell you this. I realized and found out that he was from South Africa, and that was the cause of everything.
I see, sure.
That was the background---of everything.
So, finally I mentioned something -- did you read about Oslo?
Briggs
Yes.
Well, you see, what happened, he did everything to have us thrown out. We were not thrown out. We finished our contracts.
And he had arranged to replace us, have men come in, but he -- he was thrown out of the country. He was thrown out of the country: He was deported.
Yes, yes. Well, I guess --
I don't care about that. I don't judge anyone.
Right. Well, I guess that's the important thing.
Well, let's go back a little bit here.
Yes.
We're jumping ahead here.
Sure.
I want to get some of this early stuff down here before we get too
Briggs
far away from it.
Uh-huh. Yes, sure.
How did you then get into music. How did you start playing?
Well, I tell you, it was when I went up to New York. I explained that my sister, Mrs. Edith Inez Briggs Hall--
Right.
Was housekeeping with a lady by the name of Mrs. Spooner.
But you had started studying in Charleston, right?
Oh yes, oh, yes, I'd studied with Mr. Mikell.
And how did that happen to work. You just decided you wanted to play something and --
No, my sister sent for me.
I see.
I had lost my parents, you see.
Briggs 23
Oh, your parents had died?
Died, yes. And my sister sent for me, my older sister sent for me to come out there.
But you had been studying before your parents died?
Oh, yes. With Mr. Mikell.
And studied what, the cor-net?
Cor-net, and snares.
Snares.
Snares were first. Then cor-net after. Cor-net and peck horn.
Right, and so forth.
Yes.
And how old were you then, at that time?
About twelve.
About twelve?
Yes.
Briggs
And that is -- you were just studying straight concert music? I guess there wasn't any jazz yet at that time.
I played straight concert music, and folk songs, and you know --
Right.
Well, did you hear the Jenkins Orchestra Band at that time when you were down there?
Oh, I didn't --
You never did hear it?
No, I never never did hear them. My first time I heard them was in New York.
I see.
It was on the street.
After you came up to New York?
Yes.
Well, what kind of
Briggs
Well, they were playing marches, and ragtime, and everything else.
Were they pretty good?
Pretty good.
They were?
Yes. Pretty good, yes.
Not great?
No, just one of those things, some of the boys you realized had proper control of their instruments.
Yes.
Some of them had.
Yes.

But I realized after and I found out when I met Patrick---cousins--- that the boys, they said, we were just more or less interested in trying to hide a few nickles and dimes, so we can have a proper meal.
Briggs
I see.
That goes a long way. That means a whole lot. I don't want to say what I've heard about the group and everything else.
Right.

But Patrick's cousins and I were very very good friends, very close together, all brass men were close, and that hurt me ever so much when they said we have to -- in other words, they're saying, in other words, if Herbert Wright did what he did, it wasn't really his fault, 'cause he had a rough time coming up. Herbert Wright, you know who that is?
Well, no, tell me.
Herbert Wright was a drummer from Charleston with the 369th --
He was the one who killed -- right -- James Reese.
Right.
Briggs 27
Okay, so you came up to New York in what year?
And your parents had what, both died near the same --
More or less. Yes, an average of about two years difference.
I see.
And I came up to New York.
And you lived with your older sister then?
My older sister, she is still alive.
She is.
Oh yes, she is.
In New York?
Yes, she's in a nursing home in -- what is it, the Bronx -- what's the name of it Capital Parkway, what's the name of it?
Pelham Parkway?
Briggs
Pelham Parkway.
Yes.
She's in a nursing -- she sold her home when I went back in '74, to one of her grandsons.
Yes, the boy I told you about in one of my letters who is also a jazz historian.
Yes.
I think he is still with Arlene Francis' show, at WOR.
Really.
That we all are. Yes. That's where he was when I was there. He made a what you call, a show. We had Doc Cheatham to be on the show.
Right.
Where was I?
So then when you came to New York in 1912, and you were then, what, nine years old, I guess.
No, no, I was eleven.
Eleven years old.
Briggs
And then you began -- were you going to school there, in New York?
Yes, I went to school, yes. There on 135th Street.
And you lived right there.
134th Street.
And where?
24 West 134th Street.
What's that, Seventh Avenue? Is that Lenox Avenue?
Lenox Avenue, yes, between Lenox and Fifth.
Right. Right up there where the Schomburg thing is --
Right. Not far from the Lenox Casino, the old Lenox Casino.
Right.
Do you know it?
No, I don't know it.
Yes, and Mr. -- what's his name, Mr. Spooner, he was a famous pianist,
Briggs

we had a conversation and I told him about my musical background. He was very surprised that, you know --. He said, 'Well, look, you're a kid, and I can take you to someone who could probably help you to continue your studies.'
So he took me to Mr. Glaudius Marshall, who was a choirmaster, organist and conductor of the St. Marks 138th Street -- What do you call it -- Brass Band.
The church had a brass band?
Yes, yes, yes. We all had a brass band.
The churches all had brass bands?
Oh yes.
What was that, to keep the kids out of trouble sort of --
I guess it must have been something about it, 'cause it was an awfully nice thing.
After meeting Mr. Glaudius Marshall
Briggs
who introduced me to the Martin Smith School -- do you remember Martin Smith?
No, I don't know that either.
You're too young.
Right.

(Laughter). Yes, well, he take me to the Martin Smith School and in the meanwhile, as he was in charge of the brass band, I became affiliated with the brass band. He said, 'Come on, Arthur,' you know.
And after testing my sight reading and everything, I became a member as a kid.
You played coronet?
Oh, yes.
Well, what kind of music was being played in New York at that time?
Medleys -- you're talking about jazz music?
Well, in general, 'cause
Briggs

there couldn't have been much jazz. You see the thing is, the point is, I mentioned this number, "I Wish I Could Shimmy Like My Sister Kate," and, "How Are You Gonna Keep Them Down on the Farm," and things like that.
Those were the numbers that was more or less popular, you see, popular numbers. When we played at the dance school, we played them as one-steps.
Well, you had arrangements of these?
Oh, yes. Yes, we had stock arrangements.
And you had "Sister Kate," even then?
Yes, yes.
Yes, yes. No, wait a minute. That was after 1912, a little after 1912.
A little after.
Briggs
After 1912. I was more or less, say around about fifteen then.
I see.

I was fifteen. And I'm just talking and talking and talking -- When I played "Sister Kate," I was fifteen and a half, almost sixteen, 'cause I became a member of the 369th when I was sixteen, and that's when Lt. Simpson was commissioned to sign musicians to replace Jim Europe's band leaving.
Okay, let me get that straight. I'm a little confused about what actually is happening here. So, the bands at that time, like your church band, were they playing ragtime arrangements.
Not in the church.
Not in the church band.
We played what you call, "church music".
Briggs
I see.
Church music.
But you would play in the church?
Yes, I played in church as well.
Right.
You had to. You had brass, you had trombones, you had trumpets, you had violins, many violins, violas, and everything else.
You know. A church -- you know, a regular orchestra, organist -- you have an organist.
But this wasn't in church on Sunday.
Church on Sunday, you had it with the choir.
Right.
You had choir rehearsals and things.
But then outside, I
Briggs
mean around were you hearing, I mean were ragtime piano players around. Did you hear all that or what was the --
No, at the time what I heard was more or less a pianola --
Right.
Do you remember what a pianola is?
Sure.

Mr. Marshall was also a pianist, but he was not what you would call a "ragtime piano player." He played ragtime but it was for the dance schools and everything. I'm trying to think -- yes, I did know and did hear one wonderful piano player. His name was Lucky Roberts.
Lucky Roberts?
Right.
Yeh, Lucky Roberts, and I never played with him, but he was a member of the Amsterdam and the Clef clubs.
Briggs
Okay, tell me about that. The Clef Club was really very important in those days --
Very, very important. The Clef Club was more or less like -- the Amsterdam as well, but on a lesser scale -- they were more like booking offices.
Yes.
You see, musicians would go to the Clef Club and become members and almost live in the club. You know --
They had a building?
They had a building, yes. It was 52nd Street, almost touching the El.
The Sixth Avenue El?
Yes, the Sixth Avenue El. On 52nd Street.
52nd Street?
Uh, huh. And, the musicians they would go
Briggs
to the Clef Club around about mid-day, and stay all day until a gig comes in or if it doesn't come in, no matter what, a gig or anything else, you see.
Right.
And the work that they had, it was more or less a type of society work. I don't mean society music. Playing for what you call the "smart set".
Right.
People who had, you know— And they had all that tied up. If they had too much work then they would turn some of the work over to the Amsterdam.
Well, the Amsterdam was what, that was a black club as well?
A black club as well, yes. A black club -- the Amsterdam was a black club of lesser importance.
For fellows who couldn't get into the Clef they would get into
Briggs
the Amsterdam.
Oh you would get into the Amsterdam before you would --
Work your way up to the Clef?
Yeh.
Now as I understand it, and you can correct me obviously, if I'm wrong here.--
Yes.
As I understand it, up until around that time, the black musicians had most of the work sewed up and then the white players came in later; is that right?
Yes, I think you're right, because -- yes, I think you're right. It seems just what I said about the Clef Club, they had so much work, they'd turn it over to the Amsterdam.
They had everything, so who provided most of their work, I don't know. It probably was an evolution, 'cause contrary
Briggs
to what most people think, the black musicians were not musicians at all. In my time, if you couldn't read you didn't have a chance.
Right.

To play dance schools and things, you had to read. You had what you call the stock arrangements, you get it from the editors, and you had to read it. If you couldn't read, you didn't have a chance. I believe that the majority of the guys who have bad impressions were those who had not had any instrumental training, instrumental or musical training.
Right.
That is the tonic solfege, everything.
Right.
You see, that's what I'm saying.
Right.
But in my time, as I
Briggs
said in my reference to the Lincoln Theater, you ever heard of it --
Oh yes, sure.

Well, you see, that's how it happened. And we had two or three movie picture houses that had small orchestras and the same thing happened there. Phone so and so and says, "He's sick today, could you send me a trumpet or a violin or a viola or something violin cello or something." So, you see that if you couldn't read it's another thing.
So you're expected to just go right out there and sight-read the job?
Yes. That's it, yes. And I'm very thankful to Mr. Eugene Mikell for giving me a very good theoretical musical education. I continued naturally.
You started right off as a reader?
Right.
Briggs
So it wasn't like those early jazz players in New Orleans, a lot of them couldn't read.
That's right, couldn't read, no.
But you were a trained musician.
Yes, yes, that's the difference, you see.
Right.
Yes.
Well, tell me about that, what happened then that the white guys began to move in and take over a lot of that work.
Well, I'll tell you what happened. The white boys had theoretical training. The majority of them studied harmony.
Right.
And everything else. They were permitted to go to conservatories.
Briggs
And they studied and everything, and this is the truth, they would come around and listen to certain formations, colored formations playing, and jot down certain things that they hear.
Right. I see.
And use the same, and develop their own ideas with it.
I see.

You see, they had background, they knew what they were doing. Today, if you can't arrange, if you don't know your keys, all your keys, you can't be a professor, you can't teach. You have to know everything in order to teach pupils. And that the majority didn't have. And I was fortunate when I went to London with Mr. Cook with the orchestra, through Mr. Jenkins, I shall never forget Edmund Jenkins, regardless of his Dad, God bless his soul -- Edmund Jenkins came over to the
Briggs

Syncopated Orchestra, and he knew the other two other boys, one a trumpet and the other a trombone, it was the thing they got along pretty nicely, and after -- I'm not trying to throw flowers at myself. But he probably thought that -- he heard the orchestra, he heard me play and he thought that I needed a helping hand, you see.

So, he suggested to me, he said, "Would you like to continue your studies?" I said, "Sure, I certainly will." I said, "Gee, I had a teacher in New York, he was a Frenchman, he was the first trumpet player at the Hippodrome Theater."
I was recommended to him, and I had one lesson, first lesson, $5.00.
In those days --
It was a lot of money.
A whole family of ten people could live almost a month. (Laughter).
(Laughter).
Briggs

That was my little savings from my dance schools, you know, and gigs and things, playing more or less, twice, as I said, almost twice a week, I replaced Dewitt Martin who was an excellent cornet player. Excellent, but he was always drunk. You see. And it was through my savings and everything, that I managed to pay. I took two lessons. I went back a second time. Because I went to hear him play at the Hippodrome Theater and he was a very fine cornet player -- trumpet player.
Well, the Hippodrome Theater was where?
Well, look, it was the last place I played with Noble Sissle's orchestra in 1931 before we came over, came back the last time.
Right.
I'm trying to think of where it's at, 'cause one of my, -- what do you call -- brother-in-law -- what do you call
Briggs
him, he's not a brother-in-law, he married one of my nieces. He heard me at the Hippodrome Theater with Noble Sissle's orchestra in 1930, and I'm trying to think -- it was around Broadway somewhere.
Broadway somewhere.
It was in midtown, yes, midtown.
Well, this teacher of yours was white then?
Yes, Mr. Dumont, yes. Yes, he was white. I didn't think much of him for charging that price.

I had two good lessons, really two good lessons, but in those days, a lesson shouldn't cost -- didn't cost, -- I mean, if you get the best professor on earth in New York, it wouldn't be over $1.00. In those days.
Right.

Well, the Salle de Pleyel concert was kind of a break for you --
It was a break.
It was good exposure.
Oh yes, yes. 'Cause we made the other recordings after. We made the other recordings after the Salle de
Briggs
Pleyel.
I see.
We made the other recordings after the Salle de Pleyel. Then, Panassie -- Canetti, started booking the orchestra.
But the point is, you see, he had us all sign a contract on a parietal basis, but on the parietal basis, we didn't know what his parietal was, you see.
Parietal means that you can't -- with a big orchestra, you can't -- you must have a certain sum, and then divide into parietal --
Right.
You understand?
Yes.
But he just wanted us to sign, well, you get the 10/15th or or 10/20th or something, you know -- and he didn't know.
Then, we realized after that there
Briggs
was something wrong between Canetti and some kind of a secret engagement, arrangement between Freddy and Canetti.
You mean Freddy Johnson.
Right. Some of the boys found that out. Exactly who it is, I tell you it was-- he has -- and the majority of them have all passed, now.

Sterling Conaway, one of our best guitar players, and one of the most true blues you can find, and then he came back, and he told us, he said, "I have the proof," and that caused a little dissension in the orchestra.
And, Canetti had made many arrangements, and the majority of us, we had jobs, you see. We were all working somewhere.
I was still at Bricktop's and doubling at Ciro's, and he was in some other
Briggs

club, but they all had jobs.
And they had quit their jobs
to go on the road with Canetti and then
Freddie's set up.
Well, it was Freddie's leadership? Freddie was the leader?
Yes. It was Arthur Briggs -- Freddie Johnson and then Arthur Briggs, but you have to have one man fronting, you see.
Right.

Freddie's intention was to more or less, to imitate Duke Ellington, but he couldn't, because Duke Ellington built his band around him. And that's a different thing, you see.
Duke Ellington's band without -- with another piano player, wouldn't sound the same way.
Right.
It's just the same as Count Basie's orchestra with another piano
Briggs
player, it wouldn't sound the same way, you see.
Right.
And Freddie had had the same idea of being a Duke Ellington, and having the Harlemites around him, but it wasn't -- it couldn't be the same, you see.
And after Sterling Conaway found out what was going on, the majority of the boys said they're not going to quit their jobs to take a chance on a wild goose chase, you see.

And, we had several engagements in Belgium and Holland, and every place else, that had to be cancelled. I don't know whether Canetti had to pay a duty -- or they had to pay a fine or something, I don't know.
But, it didn't interest me, because in the way that they had arranged the contract, that he and Freddie -- Conaway said that he had heard Freddie telling his wife; he said,
Briggs
"Darling, when I come back, that trunk will be stacked with 1,000 franc bills," you see.
Yes, I see.
And that's the wrong way. If you're going to do something together, do it together or not.
Surely, Freddy wanted to make some money. We all wanted to make some money. We were thinking of making a reputation doing something.
But he thought of one thing, just knocking out everybody, and taking everything for himself. That was all, with Canetti.
Well, this band -- in other words, even when it wasn't just the records, but when you were on the road, you were getting just a share -- and you never really knew what the.--
Yes, yes. And I'll tell you something about the recording. We never got a dime.
Briggs
You never got a dime?
Not a dime. My satisfaction is to listen to the recordings. (Laughter).
Right. Well, it sounds as if Canetti was a bit shrewd; right.
Yes, he was. And Freddy was with him. They worked together.
I see.

I didn't want to think so, but I was forced to think so, after that. Freddy and I, we were still great friends, when he came back, in '53 or '54, when he came back with Quincy Jones' orchestra. He was rehearsing a show. Quincy Jones brought over a show, and Freddy was the rehearsal piano player. We were still good friends. I went
Briggs 322

to his hotel and went down to see him at Alhambra Theater . He introduced me to Quincy Jones, and my boy that's just a wonderful trumpet player, today that takes it all. He was with Duke Ellington for a while --
Clark Terry?
Clark Terry, yeh.
I saw him last summer. We had dinner together. And Freddy introduced me to Clark Terry, and a whole bunch -- we had a wonderful -- nice time.
And it seems as though he regretted it, 'cause he said to me, he said, "Art, if I could live my life over again, I'd do it differently." 'Cause he realized that he had made a mistake.

We all had a chance -- we were doing something -- you know, for us, in our profession, for the love of our profession, and we had to live, but I mean, we all had a right, -- we all spent our time in rehearsals
Briggs 323
and everything else, in trying to do something together, and why -- I can't understand.
Well, how long did the band go on, before it broke up?
Well, we stayed together for -- just to make those recordings, 'cause after, after we finished the recordings, that's when we were supposed to go on the road.
That was what -- just like -- only until the band could --
No, that was six months.
Six months, that was all it was.

Yeh, we played at Salle de Pleyel, six months, and when they made all the bookings and everything else, they had no band, the boys refused to leave their jobs. They had no bands. Did I tell you about Freddy yet? He signed a contract -- I don't know
Briggs
whether Canetti was in on the deal, but he signed a contract for The Hague, in Amsterdam -- no, The Hague in Holland, at Tabariss Cabaret, dancehall cabaret.
He took most of the orchestra with me, but he knew I wasn't going. He knew it was finished, that I was not going to leave my job.
I still had my Ciro's job going, and I did not intend to go after I found out what was what. Yet, he proposed me.

And he went. He had taken another trumpet player and he went, and the following day I had a phone call from Mr. Brauer(7) who was the proprietor of the place, asking me, -- he said, "What happened?" "Mr. Johnson said that you were ill, and that you would be here in about a week or so, as soon as you're better."
And I said, there's no question, I said, "Mr. Johnson knew that the orchestra had folded." I said, "You don't have two men
Briggs

of the original orchestra with Mr. Johnson." I said, "But, if you're satisfied with it, just go ahead." So you see, those are the things -- it's a pity, 'cause we did something, when we had the first prize, awarded first prize in 1935, for "Best Recording of the Year." The world over. With those two numbers -- did I tell you, "Harlem Bound," and "Harlem Madness".
Okay, let me just try and get this straight, now.
When that thing broke up -- you were still recording into 1934 then?
Yes, uh huh.
So you made a first record in '33. And then most of the rest of these?
Yes, yes.
I see. But you were still speaking with Freddy?
Oh, yes, we were
Briggs

still -- surely, yes, but then he went to Holland. He went to Holland because Bricktop -- Pete du Conge, also found out, 'cause Sterling Conaway kept it more or less secret, you see, and didn't want any dissensions.
Pete only found out at the last moment, and he had taken it in a pretty bad manner. He told his wife, 'If you don't throw him out, I'll throw him out.' That's when Freddie decided to go to Holland.
So Freddie left and went to Holland?
Yes, went to Holland, yes.
Well, it's just one of those things that happened. But when he told me, I'm glad he said, 'If I had my life to live over, I would do it differently.'
Yeh.
I guess he realized
Briggs
he made a mistake, and the funniest thing is I told you yesterday, that Doc Cheatham, came over, three days before World War II was declared.
Doc Cheatham came over, passing France for through Holland to join Freddy, you see.
Well, just to follow that out a little bit, Freddy went back during the war, I mean right before the war.
No, no. Freddy was caught in Germany, and in Holland.
He was.
Freddy was caught in Holland --
Well, Doc turned around and got right out of there, didn't he?
Oh, yes, I told the Doc, I went down to see him. He phoned and went down to see him, and I said, 'You get
Briggs 328
the first boat back to where you came from." And he went back.
Freddy was a -- Freddy had a lot of -- I heard that Freddy had a lot of trouble in Holland, 'cause he had his wife and two children with him, two daughters, and apparently he had neglected them.

And his wife -- the Germans were already in Holland, but America was not at war, and his wife went to the police station, to the police, and she told them, that Freddy had disbanded them. You know, he didn't take her.
And, apparently, the Germans forced him to take care of his wife and children. And -- I don't know how that happened.
We are going to go back to London, briefly, to pick up a couple of things, we missed earlier, on the concert in London that Mr. Briggs wants
Briggs
tell us about.
This was a concert that was given in --
This was a concert given in honor of Coleridge-Taylor. It was called "A Coterie of Friends".
And this was at the time that you were in London, with the Southern Syncopated Orchestra?
Certainly. And the concert was on Sunday, December 7th, 1919, at 3:00 p.m., at the Whigmore Hall on Whigmore Street, West London.

I want to tell you a few words, about "A Coterie of Friends," which represented dignitaries from the British Empire, who had come to London, to be recompensed for their efforts to the Empire, during World War I.
It so happened, that these members were all dignitaries, very big persons, officials, of the Empire, all races of men.
Briggs 330
They were very surprised and humiliated by the bitter negligence of the official authorities towards them. Their reception was ice cold, as we'd say.
So, with the aid of Mr. Latimore, and Dad Cook--Will Marion Cook -- and the dignitaries, they formed "A Coterie of Friends," which represented a cultural society of brotherhood.
This concert was organized entirely by Mr. Edmund T. Jenkins who was the president of this society.
He was the son of Daniel Jenkins?
And he was the son of Daniel Jenkins, the organizer of the Jenkins Orphanage in Charleston, South Carolina.
They honored Coleridge-Taylor, and I'd like my friend Mr. Cartier to leave the program to you --
I have the xerox
Briggs 331

copy of the program, in front of me, and they were primarily the conversations with Coleridge-Taylor, and they were, "Symphonic Variations on an African Aire", a song, "Hiawatha's Vision," solos by W.A. Mikell, "Scenes from an Imaginary Ballet", "Concerto In G-Minor." The soloist was Winifred Small. "A Monologue; the Clown and Columbine," with violin-cello and piano accompaniment. Gwendolyn Coleridge-Taylor --
She was what, the pianist on the --
Yes, she was the pianist.
And then there was a "Folk Rhapsody", which was written by Edmund T. Jenkins. And then two songs by Coleridge-Taylor, "A Son of the Sea," and "Beat, Beat, Drums".
And concluded with, "The March Ethiopia, Saluting of Colors."
And the orchestra was conducted
Briggs 332
by Edmund Jenkins.
But we had four members of the Syncopated Orchestra which (Unintelligible).
Right. Well, the orchestra -- the members of the orchestra were drawn primarily from the Royal --
The Royal Academy.
The Royal Academy --
Conservatory.
Conservatory. But they did include four members of the Southern Syncopated Orchestra.
Mr. Salmavee, is it pronounced?
Salnave.
Salnave, S-a-l-n-a-v-e.
Mr. Rivera, the bass.
Mr. Rivera, the bass.
Mr. Withers.
Mr. Frank Withers, on trombone, and, of course, Mr. Arthur
Briggs
Briggs, on trumpet.
Thirty members.
Thirty members of the orchestra. And that concert, again, according to the program notes, was December 7th, 1919.
Yes.

Now, we also have another program, we want to put onto the record, which I have in my pocket. This is a concert given by the Southern Syncopated Orchestra, and this was their regular program, so this isn't dated. But these were when they were playing in Philharmonic Hall on Great Portland Street in London. Programs at 2:45 and 8:30. The orchestra, of course, is under the direction of Will Marion Cook. And in this particular program, the songs were 'Swing Along', which is one of Cook's songs, 'Hungarian Dance, No. 5,'
Briggs 334

by Brahms. A medley of traditional tunes, "Go Down Moses", "Jesamin" and "Good News", Double Quartet, "Call of the Woods," -- that was the double quartet. Then there was an orchestral piece, "Call of the Woods," I see. Then there was a solo, "Swanee River" by Miss Lottie Gee..
Yes.

Then a plantation medley by the orchestra. Then, "I Gotta Robe", which again would have been a spiritual, sung by Carol Morgan. "Ramshackle Rag," by the orchestra. "Listen to the Lambs," of course a famous concert piece, by MRS H.K. Rieves, who was singing it, that is to say. "Exhortation" by Joe Porter. That was written by Will Marion Cook. Porter was obviously the singer --
Yes, the singer.
Then Ms. Lottie Gee
Briggs
and the quartet, doing "Mammy of Mine", which is by Maclo Pinkard.
Then the orchestra did "Swanee Ripples." That was a rag, I suppose?
Yes, right.
Then after the end of double quartet to "Deep River", and the orchestra did "Moanin' Trombone", which is a trombone specialty piece.
Joe Caulk sang "Mammy". The orchestra played "Russian Rag". Then a quartet did again a medley of "Mother of Mine", "Me, Oh Lord", and "Peaches Down In Georgia".
The orchestra played "Humoresque" and "Admiration". Then Miss Gee sang "Little Gal". Henry Saparo sang "Dixieland in France".

And then, obviously one of the high points of the program at that time, as I remember, Sidney Bechet played "Characteristic Blues", as a clarinet solo and accompanied by the orchestra, playing, I suppose, just
Briggs
figures behind the solo.
Yes, yes.

And then the Jubilee Quartet, sang "Tishomingo Blues", which I always thought was a Duke Ellington tune, but obviously is not, and "Jadda". Then there was an orchestral piece, "'Mid the Pyramids", and then the program was concluded by Will Marion Cook's composition, "Rain Song", played also by the orchestra. This program would have been very typical of the kind of thing it did --
Oh, certainly.
The Southern Syncopated Orchestra.
Did you mention about the command performance that we had before the King and Queen?
No, I don't think so, why don't you speak about that.
Yes, well, I don't
Briggs
remember the date, but we had a command performance before the King and Queen at Buckingham Palace.
At Buckingham Palace, was it?
Yes. And it was about five days before the Coleridge-Taylor concert.
That would have been roughly around the beginning of December 1919?
Yeh, yeh, uh huh.
Okay. We've got those on the record now. Okay, we've come up to the war then?
Yes.
And the obvious question that comes up is why you chose to stay here, once you knew there was going to be a lot of trouble.
Well, yes, I personally did not believe that the French
Briggs
army was so weak. I thought that it would -- after World War I, they would make a much better stand, you see.
I had full confidence. And a certain reason is that my wife being Belgian, I thought I'd stay. You see, my wife, she didn't care so much for going back to the States.

Under those circumstances, 'cause we would both be, we said, 'not deported' but we would be sent back -- I had not much money -- plenty money to pay my fare, but if I went back, I would have gone back with the other boys that went back, were sent back by the Co[nsul], and then they would have a pretty difficult time to try to come back to France after the War if they wanted to, you see.
I see.
So, I decided to stay, but I paid [for it] (Laughter).
Well, when had you
Briggs
gotten married?
Huh?
When were you married?
I was married way back in '30, before I went to America.
And your wife, what was your wife's name?
Her name was Georgina Dagenner Briggs.
Dagenner was --
Dagenner, because she was Belgian. D-a-g-e-n-n-e-r.
So by this time you had been married for almost ten years?
Yes, and I --
Were you a French citizen then?
No, no.
Still American?
I only became a French citizen after, way back in '55.
Briggs
I see, I see. So you stayed here, and you just assumed that the French were going to be able to hold out?
Yes. That's all, yes.
And then everything collapsed, in 1940?
Yes.
And you hadn't continued to work as a musician?
No.
That stopped when?

That stopped, immediately. I had many propositions to work, but I did not work, because I knew that I would not be permitted to work. And the attitude of the French musicians didn't encourage me to try to work.
Well, what was that?
The attitude of the French musician was entirely hostile to
Briggs 341
knowing the German mentality, with certain people, they had just taken advantage of it, you see.

I had propositions -- that is when the Germans came in I was at the Club Pierre Charon on the Champs Elysee, and the proprietor sent for us to come back after the Germans left. And when I went down to the Consulate, the Consul told me that it would be best to stay undercover.
He told us all, those who stayed, 'cause there were quite a few that stayed, to stay undercover. We explained that we had work and everything. He thought, Mr. Murphy --
This is the American Consul?
The American Consul. His name was Mr. Murphy, a rather well known diplomat. He advised us to stay undercover, 'cause he was right.
He said, "Do you have enough money
Briggs 342

to live?" We said, "Yes, we do." And he said, "Well, stay undercover," he said, "Go in the streets only when you have to." And that's what I did until Japan -- But before then, something had happened. I showed you a picture yesterday of Aime Barelli.
Right.
Aime Barelli came back to Paris. He was from Nice.
Barelli, you should explain.

He came back as a beaten soldier, more or less. He had nothing and he had no where to go. He didn't know anybody in Paris, but he went to the local, and asked where he could find me. They gave him an address and he came up to see me.
I should just interrupt and say, that Barelli was one of
Briggs 343
the finest of the French jazz musicians.
Oh, yes, one of the finest. He spent thirty years at "The Sportin'" in Monte Carlo, and he was just reinstated about six months ago.
He had finished and he was reinstated about six months ago.

And Aime and I were great, great friends, when I first met him in 1935, and I was at the casino in Cannes, and he used to come over with his group after they finished at their casino in Nice, and sit in the cabaret, and listen to the orchestra.
Well, he was such a fine boy, he came to see me. And his first words were, "Arthur, I'm here."

I said, "I'm glad you're here". (Laughter). I said, "I'm glad you're here, glad to see you Aimé." And he said, "Yes, but I know no one, and I have no place to go." I said, "You don't have to worry," I said, "But have you got your mouthpiece?"
Briggs 344
He said, "Yes, I have it, it's the only thing that I have." He took it out. He said, "It's the only thing I saved." He was in a beaten up uniform, so I gave him a civilian outfit and everything.
And he said, "But I have to live." So I said, "Well, look, for the time being you just camp -- the best way, you camp here with me, until I see Charles Delaunay, and you'll certainly find work."

He said, "But I got no instrument." I said, "Yes, you have." "That's mine, now that's yours." So I gave it to him. I said, "I'm through with it for the time being. I'm through and you'd honor my horn," I said. I said, "I know, 'cause I've heard you play, and you'll honor my horn." I said, "It's yours."
So he took my horn and the following day we went down to Hot Club of France together, and fortunately Charles Delaunay was there.
The Hot Club is in
Briggs
Rue Chaptal 14e.
Rue Chaptal 14e.
14 Rue Chaptal 14e.
That same building
Yes, the same place, yes.
You were living where, at that time?
Not far from here, Rue Felixiene, number 7. Say about 500 yards from this apartment.
Right.

And I'd taken him down to where, Charles Delaunay was there, and other members, and they said, 'Well, we'll do all we can for him.' They found him work and everything else. And he came up to my house whenever he wanted to, and we got along nicely.
Until the 7th of December,-- they didn't lose much time, 'cause everything was arranged, they knew where everyone was,
Briggs 346
you know.
In other words, they, the Germans knew where all the Americans were
Yes, they knew where all the allies --
Everybody were.
Everybody.
And, in the morning, we didn't even know that Japan had attacked the United States. We didn't know much. We found out when the Gerries came to pick us up.
They just came right up, on December 7th, they just turned up?
Yes. And at 9:00 o'clock in the morning.
9:00 o'clock in the morning.
9:00 o'clock in the morning. Yes, they just came and picked us up. Well, it was just one of those things.
Briggs
We're still alive. I'm still alive.
You were then interned where?

At Creteil. They first sent us to Compiegne. And I stayed at Compiegne, say about a week. Because, there was another Allied camp, where they had a group of about thirty amateur musicians, and as you know, the only type of music we could play then was light music and symphonies and things. That was the only music that was permitted by the Germans. And they had in this camp, they had about a thirty-piece orchestra, but they claim that they didn't have satisfaction with the brass or the trumpets, 'cause they were more or less amateurs, you see.
Right.
And the person who was leading the band, he knew me, and he knew of my internment, and he asked the Germans to give me a transfer.
Briggs

I was then transferred to this camp in Creully, where I stayed. I had no problem 'cause I told the Germans when I got to the camp and saw what they were dishing out for food, I said, "I couldn't blow my instrument on that."

So at the abouer -- an abouer is a German office, And the officer, he was a man of a certain age, he was certainly of the old stock, 1914 stock. He was awfully nice. He said, "Look, what can I do for you, Mr. Briggs?" I said, "Well, look, I do not want work in the kitchen, but I'd like to eat with the kitchen folks. He said, "Is that all you'd like Mr. Briggs?" I said, "Yes." He said, "Well, you know, you have quite a lot of work anyhow, 'cause you have to -- now, in order -- I'll do that for you, but I would like you to blow the 'Reveille' in the morning, and at breakfast, and for a check-up
Briggs
and everything --" Four calls a day.
Right.
"That's fine," I said, "But how do I know that it works." He said, "In ten minutes it will be on the board." (Laughter).
So, that's what happened.
And I was committed to the kitchen staff, as I said, just for eating, you see. And that was pretty good. 'Cause they worked. They worked hard and they deserved to have what they had.
And I guess that's one of the reasons why I'm here today. Of course, my wife came to see me whenever she could, and she brought me a hot meal, whenever she could, as well.
But, by, (in a while) we had the Commandant of Paris, it came up and we gave a concert. It was more or less a Beethoven festival.
A Beethoven festival?
Briggs
Yes, the famous Fifth Symphony.
Right.

And the Commandateur of Paris, his name was General Von Stulpnagel. He was the Commander of Paris. The Parisian regent. And he came up, and with all his staff officers and everything, and they were very surprised, 'cause I was about the only inkspot on the stand. (Laughter). And they were very surprised because that party, they believed that everything that was not Caucasian, of the Caucasian race, was a monkey or something else, you see. (Laughter).
Right.
You see. And when they realized different, at the end of the concert, the Aide de Camp, shook my hand. And the General saluted.
Really.
Yes.
Briggs
So, I felt pretty good. I said, 'Well, maybe I'll be spared.' (Laughter) It's by choice of God, I guess, that I'm here.
Were these people all made to work, or -- was it a work camp was it?
No, no. It was not the same. We were internees.
Like prisoners of war.
Yes, war prisoners, yes.
And were there Americans and --

Yes, all together. All the Allies. Yes, all grouped together. And we're not considered as war prisoners, 'cause they couldn't force -- we would work if it was in the interest of our camp, to do things for our camp, we would work, but no one forced us to work, you see.
Briggs 352
I see. So if it was a question of building latrines or something like that --

Yeh, we'd do it ourselves, if it was necessary. But no one -- the Germans couldn't tell us, do so and so and so and so. Everything was organized like a little city, you see. A country within a country.
Well, what was it, all barracks or tents, or --
Yes, they were tents, more or less. Tents or small barracks were built quickly, you know.
Right. And how was it heated? It must have been pretty cold.
Yes, pretty cold. We had -- we were heated by coal stoves. We had one or two big stoves in a room. It depended on the size of the room, you see.
Briggs

And we had enough coal and everything, as far as that's concerned. And what we didn't care so much about at first, you see, we give them the cabbage soup. Cabbage soup with worms floating around on it. (Laughter).
So, you'd just scoop the worms out?

Yes, if you had nothing else to eat, you had to just scoop the worms out, and eat it. But that didn't last too long, 'cause the members of our committee forced the Germans, and as I told you, the Commander of the camp, was one of the 1418 Men of Surgage, an aristocrat. And he realized that civilians must be treated as civilians, 'cause we were civilians and not soldiers, you see.
Yes.
And that was when we did assume responsibility. We had days
Briggs 354

where we had potatoes, white potatoes, and we had what you call 'horses' heads' and everything, you know. (Laughter). You didn't eat it, but -- the potatoes were okay, and they had some white potatoes and butter, or margarina, -- it tasted pretty good. (Laughter).
Well, how long were you there?
Three years. Almost three years.
Right up to the liberation?
Right, right up to about the 27th of August. We were liberated the 20th of August.
By American troops?
Yes, American troops. Patton's.
Patton's army?
Yes, Patton's. I told you, I had two cousins
Briggs
who were with him. I didn't see them, 'cause they were not in the group that liberated us, but I mean they were in the group that continued up to the Czechoslovakian border.
And those two cousins caught up with you then, after a little while?
Oh yes, yes. They came in the fall to Paris and they contacted me. They found out where I was.
They came on furlough to Paris?
Yes, Paris, yes.
So they knew you were in Paris?
They knew I was in Paris, yes. I had a few letters while I was in the camp. We were permitted to write one letter a month, and we would receive a letter "peut-etre" I'd say about one or
Briggs
two letters a year. If you were fortunate, you'd receive three.
But, something I want to tell you that I hope the world will understand, one day is that the International Corps for Red Cross doesn't mean a thing.
No good.
No good at all.
When they visited our camp, we were closed in our rooms, so what kind of inspection -- how could they inform anyone of what's happening.
They saw no internees at all. We were confined to our rooms, enclosed. Because when they visited, the Gestapo came also to visit with them.
The Gestapo came along with the Red Cross?
Yeh, yeh, with the Red Cross. And the Red Cross, in general, were German-Swiss.
Briggs
Were German-Swiss?
Yeh, sure.
They were first German-Swiss.
Yes, that's right.
In Bern they were founded.
In Bern, yes.

Tough city. I was with Swiss. I mean I worked with Swiss and everything, and I had no trouble with them, but I mean, you're entitled to -- they're Germans, you can say anything you want. They were Germans.
Right. Well, how did you get out after the war when you picked up playing again?
Well, you see, in the camp, as we had this orchestra, we rehearsed everyday. That was a good thing.
So your chops were in pretty good shape.
Oh, yes, they were in pretty good shape for playing what you call light music, and things like that.
